analysis.one_liner: Lets taxpayers opt into a 17% flat tax and repeals estate and gift taxes.
analysis.headline: The Flat Tax Act, with 11 Republican cosponsors, was referred to two House committees the day it was introduced and never received a markup or vote before the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let any individual or business make a one-way election to leave the regular income tax and pay a flat tax instead: 19% for the first two years, then 17%. Individuals would be taxed only on wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment compensation, minus a large standard deduction, and would give up all tax credits. Businesses would pay the flat rate on income after subtracting the cost of inputs and wages. The bill would also repeal the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes and would require a two-thirds vote in either chamber to ever raise the flat rate or shrink the deductions.
analysis.who_benefits: High earners and businesses come out best. A household paying the top 39.6% rate could elect in and pay 17%; businesses could pay 17% instead of the 35% corporate rate, with immediate deduction of input costs. The largest estates benefit from full repeal of the estate and gift taxes. Middle-income filers get a large standard deduction but lose every credit, including the child credit and earned income tax credit.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, businesses, and large estates

how_it_helps.text: Electing individuals pay 19% for two years and 17% thereafter, far below the top regular rates, and are taxed only on wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment compensation — not on investment gains, which fall under the 17% business tax instead.
Electing businesses pay 17% on income after deducting the cost of business inputs and wages, and unused deductions can carry forward with interest as a credit.
The bill repeals the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes for deaths and gifts after December 31, 2013.
Individuals electing the flat tax get a large standard deduction — $32,496 for joint filers, $16,248 for singles, plus $6,998 per qualifying child, indexed to inflation.
The bill requires a two-thirds vote of the House or Senate to raise the flat rate or reduce the standard or business deductions, making the lower taxes hard to reverse with a simple majority.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury pays through lost revenue, meaning cuts elsewhere, more borrowing, or higher taxes on people who do not elect in. Electing low- and middle-income workers give up all tax credits, and the election is irrevocable, locking filers into whatever the flat tax looks like in later years.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal Treasury and credit-dependent low-income filers

drawbacks.text: Any taxpayer who elects the flat tax loses all tax credits, and the election cannot be revoked — so low- and middle-income families who qualify for the earned income tax credit or child credit could end up paying more than under current law.

Shifting high earners and businesses from rates up to 39.6% to 17%, and repealing the estate tax, would cut federal revenue; because the election is optional, only taxpayers who pay less would elect, so the revenue loss falls on the remaining taxpayers and federal spending.
The two-thirds supermajority requirement to raise the rate or trim deductions is a procedural rule not found in normal tax law, entrenching the new rates against a future simple majority.

Employers that are tax-exempt or government agencies would owe a 19% then 17% tax on the value of noncash benefits like health coverage given to employees, discouraging such benefits for government and nonprofit workers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains flow disproportionately to the top: a 17% rate on the highest incomes and on business income, and full estate tax repeal, are worth far more to high earners and large estates than the large standard deduction is worth to typical families — especially since electing families lose the credits that matter most to lower incomes. The revenue loss and the irrevocable, credit-free structure weigh against the simplification benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means and Rules Committees on the day it was introduced and sat there, without a markup or floor vote, until the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael Burgess introduced the Flat Tax Act on March 11, 2013, joined by Reps. Cole, Ross, and Forbes.
The same day, the Speaker referred it to the Committee on Ways and Means and, in addition, to the Committee on Rules.
Eleven Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrats did.
No further action was taken — no committee markup, no subcommittee action, no floor vote — through the end of the 113th Congress on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the federal Treasury kept the revenue from top rates and the estate tax, and credit-dependent working families were never exposed to the irrevocable credit-free flat tax. High earners and large estates lost the tax cuts the bill would have delivered.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal revenue kept; high earners got no cut

for.name: Rep. Michael C. Burgess
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Flat Tax Act on March 11, 2013.

for.name: Reps. Tom Cole, Dennis Ross, and Randy Forbes
for.what_they_did: Joined in introducing the bill at the request of the sponsor.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of primary jurisdiction (chaired by Rep. Dave Camp, R-MI)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no markup, no vote — leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was entirely Republican — Burgess plus 11 Republican cosponsors, no Democrats — and the bill never advanced to any vote.

industries.industry: High-income households and heirs of large estates
industries.note: Electing in means 17% instead of rates up to 39.6%, and the estate and gift taxes would be fully repealed, a benefit that concentrates on the very largest estates. The lost revenue would be made up by everyone else or by spending cuts.

Electing businesses would pay 17% instead of the 35% corporate rate, with immediate expensing of inputs and a carryforward credit for excess deductions. The public cost is the revenue given up, borne by other taxpayers and federal programs.

industries.industry: Government agencies and tax-exempt employers (hospitals, charities, universities)
industries.note: If their business elects, employers in this category would owe a 19% then 17% tax on the value of noncash benefits such as health coverage for employees, a cost other employers would not face.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax planning services
industries.note: A simple flat tax with a large standard deduction and no credits would shrink demand for itemized-deduction planning and compliance work, though the optional election would keep a dual system in place.
